problem: The chapter says a point is ordinary when P(x₀) ≠ 0 and then says p and q 'have Taylor series about x₀'. Standard textbooks also require P, Q, R themselves to be analytic at x₀ (for example polynomials, or functions with convergent Taylor series there). Without that, P(x₀) ≠ 0 alone does not guarantee p = Q/P and q = R/P are analytic.
fix: Assume P, Q, R are analytic at x₀ (polynomials are the usual case) and P(x₀) ≠ 0. Then p = Q/P and q = R/P are analytic at x₀, and a power series solution about x₀ exists.

problem: 'The lowest power in y″ fixes it' is only true for y″ − xy = 0. For a general y″ + p(x)y′ + q(x)y = 0 the constant term is 2a₂ + p(x₀)a₁ + q(x₀)a₀ = 0, so a₂ depends on a₀ and a₁; for y″ + y = 0 this gives a₂ = −a₀/2, not 0. Read generally, the trap can push a student to write a₂ = 0 wrongly.
fix: a₂ is not free: the constant term of the whole equation fixes it, 2a₂ + p(x₀)a₁ + q(x₀)a₀ = 0. In y″ − xy = 0 the equation has no y′ term and q = −x, so this reduces to 2a₂ = 0.
